intro: Eugen d’Albert, a pupil of Liszt, recorded Chopin’s Nocturne in F♯ major, Op. 15 No. 2 (Larghetto), in 1916. Wilhelm Kempff remembered d’Albert’s singing tone and a hand poised over a single black key.

sections.label: A · A♯ above the bass
sections.mNote: A curling melody above bass notes and soft chords.

sections.label: A′ · Larghetto theme, F♯ major
sections.mNote: The quick figures stop before the opening upbeat comes back.

cues.title: Opening melody, bars 1–4
cues.text: The melody begins on A♯ and rises briefly to B before descending. The left hand moves from a low bass note to chords near the tune. Chopin marks the opening sostenuto.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, upbeat and bars 1–4, marked sostenuto. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: D’Albert in Weimar, 1882
cues.text: In 1882 d’Albert went to Weimar to study with Liszt. In a letter of 14/26 July 1884 to Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky described the young pianist, whom he had heard in Moscow, as “the legitimate successor of Rubinstein”, meaning Anton Rubinstein.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Nadezhda von Meck, 14/26 July 1884; the Rubinstein named is Anton. Letter and d’Albert’s Weimar studies are documented in Mark Mitchell and Allan Evans’s notes: https://arbiterrecords.org/catalog/eugen-d-albert-the-centaur-pianist/

cues.title: Middle section, doppio movimento
cues.text: The middle section doubles the tempo. Inside the right hand, quick notes run beneath a dotted melody, and the left hand leaps between widely spaced notes. The section opens sotto voce and then grows louder.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 25–32: doppio movimento and sotto voce. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return to the opening tempo
cues.text: In bars 47–52 the repeated figures slow and fade, marked molto rallentando and smorzando. After a pause, the A♯–B turn returns a tempo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–52: molto rallentando, smorzando, a pause and a Tempo. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Kempff on d’Albert’s playing
cues.text: In his memoir Unter dem Zimbelstern, Wilhelm Kempff recalled d’Albert’s hand hovering over an A♯. To Kempff the fading note trembled like a human voice. When the passage returned, he heard a new sound from the same black key.
cues.evidence: Paraphrase of Wilhelm Kempff’s recollection in Unter dem Zimbelstern, reproduced beside the discussion of this nocturne by Mark Mitchell and Allan Evans: https://arbiterrecords.org/catalog/eugen-d-albert-the-centaur-pianist/

transitions.title: A new tune over C♯
transitions.how: The A♯s held at the end of the slow section lead into a C♯ bass. E♯, G♯ and B fill out a dominant seventh above it. The marking changes to doppio movimento, with sotto voce beneath the right hand, which now plays both a dotted melody and quick accompanying notes.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 24–26. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

transitions.title: The left hand stops before the reprise
transitions.how: A deep C♯ in the bass supports the last repeated figures, marked molto rallentando, smorzando. The left hand then stops. After a pause comes the A♯–B upbeat of the returning melody. C♯ returns in the bass, and F♯ follows in the next bar. The first tempo is restored.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–50. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
